    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">FEDERAL
AND STATE TAXATION</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Federal
Taxation</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">General</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>Oritani
Financial Corp. and Oritani Bank are subject to federal income taxation in the
same general manner as other corporations, with some exceptions discussed
below.&#160;&#160;Neither Oritani Financial Corp.&#8217;s nor Oritani Bank&#8217;s federal
tax returns are currently under audit, and neither entity has been audited
during the past five years.&#160;&#160;The following discussion of federal
taxation is intended only to summarize certain pertinent federal income tax
matters and is not a comprehensive description of the tax rules applicable to
Oritani Financial Corp. or Oritani Bank.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Method of
Accounting</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>For federal
income tax purposes, Oritani Financial Corp. currently reports its income and
expenses on the accrual method of accounting and uses a tax year ending December
31 for filing its federal and state income tax returns.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Bad Debt
Reserves</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>Historically,
Oritani Bank has been subject to special provisions in the tax law regarding
allowable tax bad debt deductions and related reserves.&#160;&#160;Tax law
changes were enacted in 1996, pursuant to the Small Business Protection Act of
1996 (the &#8220;1996 Act&#8221;), that eliminated the use of the percentage of taxable
income method for tax years after 1995 and required recapture into taxable
income over a six year period of all bad debt reserves accumulated after
1988.&#160;&#160;Oritani Bank recaptured its reserve balance over the six-year
period ended December 31, 2003.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Currently,
the Oritani Bank consolidated group uses the specific charge-off method to
account for bad debt deductions for income tax purposes.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Taxable
Distributions and Recapture</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>Prior to the
1996 Act, bad debt reserves created prior to January 1, 1988 were subject to
recapture into taxable income should Oritani Bank fail to meet certain thrift
asset and definitional tests.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">At June
30, 2009, our total federal pre-base year reserve was approximately $15.1
million.&#160;&#160;However, under current law, pre-base year reserves remain
subject to recapture should Oritani Bank make certain non-dividend
distributions, repurchase any of its stock, pay dividends in excess of tax
earnings and profits, or cease to maintain a bank charter.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Alternative
Minimum Tax</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>The Internal
Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the &#8220;Code&#8221;) imposes an alternative minimum tax
(&#8220;AMT&#8221;) at a rate of 20% on a base of regular taxable income plus certain tax
preferences (&#8220;alternative minimum taxable income&#8221; or &#8220;AMTI&#8221;).&#160;&#160;The AMT
is payable to the extent such AMTI is in excess of an exemption amount and the
AMT exceeds the regular income tax.&#160;&#160;Net operating losses can offset
no more than 90% of AMTI.&#160;&#160;Certain payments of alternative minimum tax
may be used as credits against regular tax liabilities in future
years.&#160;&#160;Oritani Financial Corp. and Oritani Bank have not been subject
to the AMT and have no such amounts available as credits for
carryover.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Net Operating
Loss Carryforwards</font><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-STYLE: italic">.&#160;&#160;</font>A financial
institution may carry back net operating losses to the preceding two taxable
years and forward to the succeeding 20 taxable years.&#160;&#160;At June 30,
2009, Oritani Bank had no net operating loss carryforwards for federal income
tax purposes.</font></div><br>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">State
Taxation</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">New Jersey State
Taxation.</font>&#160;&#160;Oritani Bank files New Jersey Corporation Business
income tax returns.&#160;&#160;Generally, the income of savings institutions in
New Jersey, which is calculated based on federal taxable income, subject to
certain adjustments, is subject to New Jersey tax.&#160;&#160;Oritani Bank is
not currently under audit with respect to its New Jersey income tax returns and
Oritani Bank&#8217;s state tax returns have not been audited for the past five
years.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">New
Jersey tax law does not and has not allowed for a taxpayer to file a tax return
on a combined or consolidated basis with another member of the affiliated group
where there is common ownership.&#160;&#160;However, under recent tax
legislation, if the taxpayer cannot demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence
that the tax filing discloses the true earnings of the taxpayer on its business
carried on in the State of New Jersey, the New Jersey Director of the Division
of Taxation may, at the director&#8217;s discretion, require the taxpayer to file a
consolidated return for the entire operations of the affiliated group or
controlled group, including its own operations and income.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">ITEM
1A.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;
&#160;&#160;&#160;<font style="DISPLAY: inline; TEXT-DECORATION: underline">RISK
FACTORS</font></font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Future
Changes in Interest Rates Could Reduce Our Profits.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
ability to make a profit largely depends on our net interest income, which could
be negatively affected by changes in interest rates.&#160;&#160;Net interest
income is the difference between:</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div>
      <table align="center" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" id="hangingindent" width="100%">
          <tr valign="top">
            <td style="WIDTH: 54pt">
              <div><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
      </font></div>
            </td>
            <td style="WIDTH: 18pt">
              <div style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline;" face="Symbol, serif">&#183;</font></font></div>
            </td>
            <td>
              <div align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">the
      interest income we earn on our interest-earning assets, such as loans and
      securities; and</font></div>
            </td>
          </tr>
      </table>
    </div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div>
      <table align="center" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" id="hangingindent" width="100%">
          <tr valign="top">
            <td style="WIDTH: 54pt">
              <div><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
      </font></div>
            </td>
            <td style="WIDTH: 18pt">
              <div style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline;" face="Symbol, serif">&#183;</font></font></div>
            </td>
            <td>
              <div align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">the
      interest expense we pay on our interest-bearing liabilities, such as
      deposits and borrowings.</font></div>
            </td>
          </tr>
      </table>
    </div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">In
addition, changes in interest rates can affect the average life of loans and
mortgage-backed and related securities.&#160;&#160;A reduction in interest rates
results in increased prepayments of loans and mortgage-backed and related
securities, as borrowers refinance their debt in order to reduce their borrowing
costs. This creates reinvestment risk, which is the risk that we may not be able
to reinvest prepayments at rates that are comparable to the rates we earned on
the prepaid loans or securities. Increases in interest rates may decrease loan
demand and/or make it more difficult for borrowers to repay adjustable rate
loans.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Changes
in interest rates also affect the current market value of our interest-earning
securities portfolio.&#160;&#160;Generally, the value of securities moves
inversely with changes in interest rates.&#160;&#160;At June 30, 2009, the fair
value of our available for sale agency securities, mortgage-backed securities
and corporate debt obligations totaled $265.6 million.&#160;&#160;Unrealized net
gains on these available for sale securities totaled approximately $3.7 million
at June 30, 2009 and are reported as a separate component of stockholders&#8217;
equity.&#160;&#160;Decreases in the fair value of securities available for sale
in future periods would have an adverse effect on stockholders&#8217;
equity.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">In
addition, many of our FHLB of New York advances are callable, often five years
from the date of issuance.&#160;&#160;To the extent the FHLB of New York calls
all or a portion of these advances, we would need to find another funding
source, which might be more expensive to us than these advances.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We
evaluate interest rate sensitivity by estimating the change in Oritani Bank&#8217;s
net portfolio value over a range of interest rate scenarios.&#160;&#160;Net
portfolio value is the discounted present value of expected cash flows from
assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet contracts.&#160;&#160;At June 30,
2009, in the event of an immediate 200 basis point increase in interest rates,
the model projects that we would experience a $70.9 million, or 29.7%, decrease
in net portfolio value.&#160;&#160;See &#8220;Item 7. Management&#8217;s Discussion and
Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations-Management of Market
Risk.&#8221;</font></div><br>
    <div id="PGBRK" style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt">
      <div id="FTR">
        <div id="GLFTR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="left"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 8pt; COLOR: #000000; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
</font></div>
      </div>
      <div id="PN" style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always">
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">37</font></div>
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center">
          <hr style="COLOR: black" noshade size="2">
        </div>
      </div>
      <div id="HDR">
        <div id="GLHDR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="right"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 8pt; COLOR: #000000; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
</font></div>
      </div>
    </div><br>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
Continued Emphasis On Multi-Family, and Commercial Real Estate Lending Could
Expose Us To Increased Lending Risks.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
business strategy centers on continuing our emphasis on multi-family, and
commercial real estate lending.&#160;&#160;We have grown our loan portfolio in
recent years with respect to these types of loans and intend to continue to
emphasize these types of lending.&#160;&#160;At June 30, 2009, $839.7 million,
or 64.6%, of our total loan portfolio consisted of multi-family loans and
commercial real estate loans.&#160;&#160;As a result, our credit risk profile
will be higher than traditional thrift institutions that have higher
concentrations of one- to four-family residential loans.&#160;&#160;Loans
secured by multi-family and commercial real estate generally expose a lender to
greater risk of non-payment and loss than one- to four-family residential
mortgage loans because repayment of the loans often depends on the successful
operation of the property and the income stream of the underlying
property.&#160;&#160;Additionally, such loans typically involve larger loan
balances to single borrowers or groups of related borrowers compared to one- to
four-family residential mortgage loans.&#160;&#160;Accordingly, an adverse
development with respect to one loan or one credit relationship can expose us to
greater risk of loss compared to an adverse development with respect to a one-
to four-family residential mortgage loan.&#160;&#160;We seek to minimize these
risks through our underwriting policies, which require such loans to be
qualified on the basis of the property&#8217;s collateral value, net income and debt
service ratio; however, there is no assurance that our underwriting policies
will protect us from credit-related losses.&#160;&#160;Finally, if we foreclose
on multi-family and commercial real estate loans, our holding period for the
collateral typically is longer than one-to four- family residential mortgage
loans because there a fewer potential purchasers of the collateral.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">The
largest commercial real estate loan in our portfolio at June 30, 2009 was a
$21.0 million loan secured by a shopping mall located in Ocean County, New
Jersey.&#160;&#160;Our largest commercial real estate relationship consisted of
properties located mainly in our primary market area with a real estate
investor.&#160;&#160;The aggregate outstanding loan balance for this
relationship is $40.9 million.&#160;&#160;As discussed in &#8220;Business of Oritani
Financial Corp-Lending Activities&#8221;, we have recently been utilizing stricter
underwriting for these types of loans, and curtailed our construction
lending.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">If
Our Allowance for Loan Losses is Not Sufficient to Cover Actual Loan Losses, Our
Earnings Will Decrease.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We make
various assumptions and judgments about the collectibility of our loan
portfolio, including the creditworthiness of our borrowers and the value of the
real estate and other assets serving as collateral for the repayment of many of
our loans.&#160;&#160;In determining the amount of the allowance for loan
losses, we review our loans and our loss and delinquency experience, and we
evaluate economic conditions.&#160;&#160;If our assumptions are incorrect, our
allowance for loan losses may not be sufficient to cover losses inherent in our
loan portfolio, resulting in additions to our allowance.&#160;&#160;Our
increased level of delinquent and nonaccrual loans increase the possibility that
this could occur.&#160;&#160;While our allowance for loan losses was 1.59% of
total loans at June 30, 2009, material additions to our allowance could
materially decrease our net income.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">In
addition, bank regulators periodically review our allowance for loan losses and
may require us to increase our provision for loan losses or recognize further
loan charge-offs.&#160;&#160;Any increase in our allowance for loan losses or
loan charge-offs as required by these regulatory authorities might have a
material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of
operations.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
Direct Investments in Real Estate May Be Riskier than More Traditional Real
Estate Loans.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Oritani
Financial Corp. and Oritani Bank each have formed companies that have invested
directly in real estate.&#160;&#160;While these investments have provided us net
income during the course of these investments, they are direct investments and
represent a greater risk than loans.&#160;&#160;With loans, the borrower has an
investment interest in the property that partially insulates the loan from the
negative consequences of decreases in the property&#8217;s value.&#160;&#160;There is
no such protection with a direct real estate investment.&#160;&#160;Any decline
in performance of these investments may have an adverse effect on our net
income.&#160;&#160;As detailed in &#8220;Business of Oritani Financial
Corp.-Subsidiary Activities and Joint Venture Information&#8221;, we have increased
our investments in these types of assets.</font></div><br>

Market and Economics Conditions May Significantly Affect Our Operations and

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Recent
negative developments in the national and global credit markets have resulted in
uncertainty in the financial markets and downturn in general economic
conditions, including increased levels of unemployment. The resulting economic
pressure on consumers and businesses may adversely affect our business,
financial condition, and results of operations.&#160;&#160;A worsening of these
conditions would likely exacerbate the adverse effects of these difficult market
conditions on us and others in the financial services industry. In general, loan
and investment securities credit quality has deteriorated at many institutions
and the values of real estate collateral supporting many commercial loans and
home mortgages have declined and may continue to decline. Indications of the
deterioration of the value of real estate collateral have been evidenced on a
national level as well as in our Market Area. These developments could have a
significant negative effect on our borrowers and the values of underlying
collateral securing loans, which could negatively affect our financial
performance.&#160;&#160;Housing market conditions in the New York metro area,
where most of our lending activity occurs, have deteriorated as evidenced by
reduced levels of sales, increasing inventories of houses on the market,
declining house prices and an increase in the length of time houses remain on
the market.&#160;&#160;The S&amp;P/Case-Shiller Home Price Indices, the leading
measure of U.S. home prices, showed that the price of existing single family
homes in the New York metro area as June, 2009, suffered a 12.0% decline versus
the prior year.&#160;&#160;RealtyTrac, a leading online marketplace for
foreclosure properties, noted in its 2008 U.S. Foreclosure Market Report that
New Jersey foreclosures in 2008 had increased 101.2% from 2007, and that the
overall foreclosure rate in New Jersey for 2008 was
1.80%.&#160;&#160;Foreclosure filings, in New Jersey in the first six months of
2009, increased 31.6% compared to the first half of 2008.&#160;&#160;Weakening
economic conditions in the residential and commercial real estate sector have
adversely affected, and may continue to adversely affect, our loan portfolio.
Total non-performing assets increased from $14.2 million at June 30, 2008 to
$52.5 at June 30, 2009, and total non-performing loans as a percentage of total
assets increased to 2.74% at June 30, 2009 as compared to 0.98% at June 30,
2008.&#160;&#160;If loans that are currently non-performing further deteriorate
or loans that are currently performing become non-performing loans, we may need
to increase our allowance for loan losses, which would have an adverse impact on
our financial condition and results of operations.&#160;&#160;The Company would
have recognized an additional $3.7 million in interest income during the year
ended June 30, 2009 had non-performing loans performed in accordance with the
original terms.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
FDIC Premium Could Be Substantially Higher In The Future Which Would Have An
Adverse Effect On Our Future Earnings .</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">On May
22, 2009, the FDIC adopted a final rule levying a five basis point special
assessment on each insured depository institution&#8217;s assets minus Tier 1 capital
as of June 30, 2009.&#160;&#160;The special assessment is payable on September
30, 2009.&#160;&#160;We recorded an expense of $846,000 during the quarter ended
June 30, 2009, to reflect the special assessment.&#160;&#160;The final rule
permits the FDIC&#8217;s Board of Directors to levy up to two additional special
assessments of up to five basis points each during 2009 if the FDIC estimates
that the DIF reserve ratio will fall to a level that the FDIC&#8217;s Board of
Directors believes would adversely affect public confidence or to a level that
will be close to or below zero.&#160;&#160;The FDIC has publicly announced that
it is probable that it will levy an additional special assessment of up to five
basis points later in 2009, the amount and timing of which are currently
uncertain.&#160;&#160;Any further special assessments that the FDIC levies will
be recorded as an expense during the appropriate period.&#160;&#160;In addition,
the FDIC materially increased the general assessment rate and, therefore, our
FDIC general insurance premium expense will increase substantially compared to
prior periods.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">If

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We own

hold the FHLB-NY common stock to qualify for membership in the Federal Home Loan
Bank System and to be eligible to borrow funds under the FHLB-NY&#8217;s advance
program.&#160;&#160;The aggregate cost and fair value of our FHLB-NY common

value.&#160;&#160;There is no market for our FHLB-NY common stock.</font></div>

could result in materially lower regulatory capital levels.&#160;&#160;In an
extreme situation, it is possible that the capitalization of a Federal Home Loan
Bank, including the FHLB-NY, could be substantially diminished or reduced to
zero.&#160;&#160;Consequently, we believe that there is a risk that our
investment in FHLB-NY common stock could be deemed other-than-temporarily
impaired at some time in the future, and if this occurs, it would cause our
earnings to decrease by the after-tax amount of the impairment
charge.</font></div><br>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We have

new branches will offset the increased expenses resulting from operating these

branches can become profitable, especially in areas in which we do not have an
established presence.&#160;&#160;During this period, the expense of operating

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Strong
Competition Within Our Market Area May Limit Our Growth and

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Competition
in the banking and financial services industry is intense.&#160;&#160;In our
market area, we compete with numerous commercial banks, savings institutions,
mortgage brokerage firms, credit unions, finance companies, mutual funds,
insurance companies, and brokerage and investment banking firms operating
locally and elsewhere. Some of our competitors have substantially greater
resources and lending limits than we have, have greater name recognition and
market presence that benefit them in attracting business, and offer certain
services that we do not or cannot provide. In addition, larger competitors may
be able to price loans and deposits more aggressively than we do. Our
profitability depends upon our continued ability to successfully compete in our
market area. The greater resources and deposit and loan products offered by some
of our competitors may limit our ability to increase our interest-earning
assets. For additional information see &#8220;Business of Oritani Financial Corp -
Competition.&#8221;</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Oritani
Financial Corp, MHC Exercises Voting Control Over Oritani Financial Corp.;
Public Stockholders Own a Minority Interest.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Oritani
Financial Corp., MHC owns a majority of Oritani Financial Corp.&#8217;s common stock
and, through its Board of Directors, exercises voting control over the outcome
of all matters put to a vote of stockholders (including the election of
directors), except for matters that require a vote greater than a
majority.&#160;&#160;Public stockholders own a minority of the outstanding
shares of Oritani Financial Corp.&#8217;s common stock.&#160;&#160;The same directors
and officers who manage Oritani Financial Corp. and Oritani Bank also manage
Oritani Financial Corp., MHC.&#160;&#160;In addition, regulatory restrictions
applicable to Oritani Financial Corp., MHC prohibit the sale of Oritani
Financial Corp. unless the mutual holding company first undertakes a second-step
conversion.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We
Operate in a Highly Regulated Industry, Which Limits the Manner and Scope of Our
Business Activities.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We are
subject to extensive supervision, regulation and examination by the New Jersey
Department of Banking and by the FDIC.&#160;&#160;As a result, we are limited in
the manner in which we conduct our business, undertake new investments and
activities and obtain financing.&#160;&#160;This regulatory structure is
designed primarily for the protection of the DIF and our depositors, and not to
benefit our stockholders.&#160;&#160;This regulatory structure also gives the
regulatory authorities extensive discretion in connection with their supervisory
and enforcement activities and examination policies, including policies with
respect to capital levels, the timing and amount of dividend payments, the
classification of assets and the establishment of adequate loan loss reserves
for regulatory purposes.&#160;&#160;In addition, we must comply with significant
anti-money laundering and anti-terrorism laws.&#160;&#160;Government agencies
have substantial discretion to impose significant monetary penalties on
institutions which fail to comply with these laws.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">A
Legislative Proposal Has Been Introduced That Would Require Oritani Financial
Corp., MHC and the Company to Become Bank Holding Companies.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">The U.S.
Treasury Department recently released a legislative proposal that would
implement sweeping changes to the current bank regulatory
structure.&#160;&#160;The proposal would create a new federal banking regulator,
the National Bank Supervisor, and merge the Office of Thrift Supervision (the
current primary federal regulator of Oritani Financial Corp., MHC and the
Company) as well as the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the primary
federal regulator for national banks) into this new federal bank
regulator.</font></div><br>
    <div id="PGBRK" style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt">
      <div id="FTR">
        <div id="GLFTR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="left"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 8pt; COLOR: #000000; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
</font></div>
      </div>
      <div id="PN" style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always">
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">40</font></div>
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center">

      <div id="HDR">
        <div id="GLHDR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="right"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 8pt; COLOR: #000000; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">&#160;
</font></div>
      </div>
    </div><br>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">If this
proposal is implemented, Oritani Financial Corp., MHC and the Company would
become bank holding companies subject to supervision by the Board of Governors
of the Federal Reserve System (the &#8220;Federal Reserve&#8221;) as opposed to the Office
of Thrift Supervision.&#160;&#160;The Federal Reserve has historically looked to
Office of Thrift Supervision regulations in its regulation of mutual holding
companies and processing of mutual holding company applications; however, it is
not obligated to follow such regulations.&#160;&#160;One important Office of
Thrift Supervision regulation that the Federal Reserve does not follow relates
to the ability of mutual holding companies to waive the receipt of dividends
declared on the common stock of their stock holding company or savings bank
subsidiaries.&#160;&#160;While Office of Thrift Supervision regulations permit
mutual holding companies to waive the receipt of dividends, subject to filing a
notice with the Office of Thrift Supervision and receiving its non-objection,
the Federal Reserve&#8217;s current policy is to prohibit mutual holding companies
from waiving the receipt of dividends so long as the subsidiary savings bank is
well capitalized.&#160;&#160;Moreover, Office of Thrift Supervision regulations
provide that it will not take into account the amount of waived dividends in
determining an appropriate exchange ratio for minority shares in the event of
the conversion of a mutual holding company to stock form.&#160;&#160;If the
Office of Thrift Supervision is eliminated, the Federal Reserve becomes the
exclusive regulator of mutual holding companies, and the Federal Reserve retains
its current policy regarding dividend waivers by mutual holding companies,
Oritani Financial Corp., MHC would not be permitted to waive the receipt of
dividends declared by the Company. This could have an adverse impact on our
ability to pay dividends and, consequently, the value of our common
stock.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">ITEM
1B.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;<font style="DISPLAY: inline; TEXT-DECORATION: underline">UNRESOLVED STAFF

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font id="TAB1" style="MARGIN-LEFT: 36pt"></font>Not applicable.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">ITEM
2.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;<font style="DISPLAY: inline; TEXT-DECORATION: underline">PROPERTIES</font></font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">At June
30, 2009, the Company and the Bank conducted business from its corporate
headquarters in Washington Township, New Jersey, and 20 full service branch
offices located in Bergen and Union Counties, New Jersey.&#160;&#160;The
aggregate net book value of premises and equipment was $13.8 million at June 30,
2009.&#160;&#160;During fiscal 2008, the Company purchased land in Bergenfield,
NJ to construct a de novo branch location that is expected to open in 2010 and
entered into a contract to lease premises in Jersey City, NJ, for the purpose of
a de novo branch location which opened in October 2008.&#160;&#160;During fiscal
year 2006, the Company sold its branch location and former Corporate
Headquarters in Hackensack, NJ to a private investor.&#160;&#160;The asset was
transferred in December, 2005 and the Company initially accounted for the
transaction as a finance obligation due to the Company&#8217;s continuing involvement
with the transferred property.&#160;&#160;The Company leased back a portion of
the premises and provided the buyer with non recourse financing.&#160;&#160;In
accordance with finance obligation accounting, the asset was not removed from
the Company&#8217;s books at that time.&#160;&#160;During fiscal year 2007, the non
recourse note was sold to another financial institution which permitted the
Company to utilize sale/leaseback accounting (as prescribed by FASB statement
No. 98) for the transaction.&#160;&#160;As a result, the former headquarters was
removed from the books of the Company and office properties and equipment, net
decreased by $1.5 million.&#160;&#160;In accordance with this guidance, a
$514,000 gain on the sale was recognized.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">ITEM
3.&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;<font style="DISPLAY: inline; TEXT-DECORATION: underline">LEGAL
PROCEEDINGS</font></font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>

Company and its subsidiaries are subject to various legal actions arising in the
normal course of business.&#160;&#160;In the opinion of management, the
resolution of these legal actions is not expected to have a material adverse
effect on the Company&#8217;s results of operations.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">On June
25, 2009, the Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of $.05 per
common share, which was paid on July 24, 2009, to common stockholders of record
as of the close of business on July 10, 2009.&#160;&#160;The Company&#8217;s Board of
Directors intends to review the payment of dividends quarterly and plans to
maintain a regular cash dividend in the future, subject to capital requirements,
financial condition, results of operations, tax considerations, industry
standards, economic conditions, regulatory restrictions that affect the payment
of dividends by the Bank to the Company and other relevant
factors.&#160;&#160;No assurances can be given that any cash dividends will be
paid or that, if paid, will not be reduced or eliminated in the
future.</font></div>

sources of funds for the payment of a cash dividend are the retained proceeds
form the initial sale of shares of common stock and earnings on those proceeds,
interest and principal payments with respect to Oritani Financial Corp.&#8217;s loan
to the Employee Stock Ownership Plan, and dividends from Oritani
Bank.&#160;&#160;For a discussion of the limitations applicable to Oritani
Bank&#8217;s ability to pay dividends, see &#8220;Supervision and Regulation&#8212;Federal Banking

    <div>
      <table align="center" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" id="hangingindent" width="100%">
          <tr valign="top">
            <td style="WIDTH: 72pt">
              <div style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">ITEM
      7.</font></div>
            </td>
            <td>
              <div align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; TEXT-DECORATION: underline">MANAGEMENT&#8217;S
      DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF
      OPERATIONS</font></font></div>
            </td>
          </tr>
      </table>
    </div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="left"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Business
Strategy</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
business strategy is to operate as a well-capitalized and profitable financial
institution dedicated to providing exceptional personal service to our
individual and business customers.&#160;&#160;We cannot assure you that we will
successfully implement our business strategy.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="left"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Highlights
of our business strategy are discussed below:</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Continuing to focus on multi-family,
and commercial real estate lending</font>.&#160;&#160;Our primary business focus
over the past several years has been the origination of multi-family, commercial
real estate, and construction loans.&#160;&#160;Although construction lending
has been curtailed due to current market and economic conditions, we have
focused on this type of lending because the interest rates earned for such loans
are higher than the prevailing rates for residential loans, resulting in greater
interest income potential.&#160;&#160;We are also able to generate significantly
higher fee income on such loans.&#160;&#160;In addition, the repayment terms
usually expose us to less interest rate risk than fixed-rate residential
loans.&#160;&#160;We generally incorporate one or more of the following features
into our terms for multi-family and commercial real estate loans, thereby
decreasing their interest rate risk: interest rates reset after five years at a
predetermined spread to treasury rates; minimum stated interest rates; balloon
repayment date or maximum fixed-rate self-amortizing loan term of 20
years.&#160;&#160;Fixed-rate self-amortizing loans are generally only offered
for loan amounts of $2.0 million or less.&#160;&#160;While we have expanded our
involvement in these loans over the past few years, we have been involved in
multi-family lending for over thirty years.&#160;&#160;Over the past six years,
we have assembled a department exclusively devoted to the origination and
administration of multi-family and commercial real estate
loans.&#160;&#160;There are presently seven loan officers in the department as
well as support staff.&#160;&#160;While our actual origination volume will
depend upon market conditions, we intend to continue our emphasis on
multi-family and commercial real estate loans.&#160;&#160;Management is
currently applying stricter underwriting guidelines to these loans,
particularity commercial real estate.&#160;&#160;These factors will also impact
origination volume.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div id="PGBRK" style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt">
      <div id="FTR">
        <div id="GLFTR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="left">
        </div>
      </div>
      <div id="PN" style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always">
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">45</font></div>
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center">
          <hr style="COLOR: black" noshade size="2">
        </div>
      </div>
      <div id="HDR">
        <div id="GLHDR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="right">
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Reduce Problem
Assets</font>.&#160;&#160;While considered more of a focus than a strategy,
management&#8217;s primary objective for the 2010 fiscal year is to reduce our level
of problem assets.&#160;&#160;Management&#8217;s focus is to secure a method to
dispose of the assets, and to maximize the economic return, considering the
current environment, upon the disposal.&#160;&#160;While no assurances can be
provided regarding results, management will focus a significant amount of its
time on the resolution of problem assets.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Maintain and increase core
deposits</font>.&#160;&#160;We have recently experienced a period of
unprecedented deposit growth.&#160;&#160;Much of the increase came in the areas
of Certificates of Deposit and Money Market accounts.&#160;&#160;Our focus for
2010 will be to build upon this success.&#160;&#160;A portion of our 2009 growth
was driven by the interest rates we offered on our deposit
products.&#160;&#160;In addition to continuing to attract new customers to the
Bank in 2010, we will also focus on cross-selling core accounts to customers who
have limited deposit services with the Bank.&#160;&#160;Such strategy will make
deposit retention less dependent on attractive interest rates.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">In
October, 2009, the Bank opened two de novo branches.&#160;&#160;These branches
had combined deposit totals of $37.8 million at June 30, 2009.&#160;&#160;We
intend to continue the strategy of opportunistic de novo
branching.&#160;&#160;We intend to open at least one new branch location in 2010
and will continue to seek additional locations.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Critical
Accounting Policies</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We
consider accounting policies that require management to exercise significant
judgment or discretion or to make significant assumptions that have, or could
have, a material impact on the carrying value of certain assets or on income, to
be critical accounting policies.&#160;&#160;We consider the following to be our
critical accounting policies.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Allowance for Loan
Losses</font>.&#160;&#160;The allowance for loan losses is the estimated amount
considered necessary to cover credit losses inherent in the loan portfolio at
the balance sheet date.&#160;&#160;The allowance is established through the
provision for loan losses that is charged against income.&#160;&#160;In
determining the allowance for loan losses, we make significant estimates and,
therefore, have identified the allowance as a critical accounting
policy.&#160;&#160;&#160;The methodology for determining the allowance for loan
losses is considered a critical accounting policy by management because of the
high degree of judgment involved, the subjectivity of the assumptions used, and
the potential for changes in the economic environment that could result in
changes to the amount of the recorded allowance for loan losses.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">The
allowance for loan losses has been determined in accordance with U.S. generally
accepted accounting principles, under which we are required to maintain an
allowance for probable losses at the balance sheet date.&#160;&#160;We are
responsible for the timely and periodic determination of the amount of the
allowance required.&#160;&#160;We believe that our allowance for loan losses is
adequate to cover specifically identifiable losses, as well as estimated losses
inherent in our portfolio for which certain losses are probable but not
specifically identifiable.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Management
performs a quarterly evaluation of the adequacy of the allowance for loan
losses.&#160;&#160;The analysis of the allowance for loan losses has two
components: specific and general allocations.&#160;&#160;Specific allocations
are made for loans that are classified.&#160;&#160;Management will identify
loans that have demonstrated issues that cause concern regarding full
collectibility in the required time frame.&#160;&#160;Delinquency is a key
indicator of such issues.&#160;&#160;In addition, the Company utilizes the
services of an external loan review firm.&#160;&#160;The loan review firm
reviews a significant portion of new originations and the existing portfolio
over the course of the year.&#160;&#160;Their scope is determined by the Audit
Committee.&#160;&#160;This firm prepares quarterly reports that include
recommendations for classification.&#160;&#160;Their services assist in
identifying loans that should be classified prior to delinquency
issues.&#160;&#160;Management summarizes all problem loans and classifies such
loans within the following industry standard categories: Special Mention;
Substandard; Doubtful or Loss.&#160;&#160;In addition, a classified loan may be
considered impaired.&#160;&#160;Impairment is measured by determining the
present value of expected future cash flows or, for collateral-dependent loans,
the fair value of the collateral adjusted for market conditions and selling
expenses.&#160;&#160;The general allocation is determined by segregating the
remaining loans by type of loan, risk weighting (if applicable) and payment
history.&#160;&#160;We also analyze historical loss experience, delinquency
trends, general economic conditions, geographic concentrations, industry and
peer comparisons.&#160;&#160;This analysis establishes factors that are applied
to the loan groups to determine the amount of the general
allocation.&#160;&#160;This evaluation is inherently subjective, as it requires
material estimates that may be susceptible to significant revisions based upon
changes in economic and real estate market conditions.&#160;&#160;Actual loan
losses may be significantly more than the allowance for loan losses we have
established, which could have a material negative effect on our financial
results.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div id="PGBRK" style="MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt">
      <div id="FTR">
        <div id="GLFTR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="left">
        </div>
      </div>
      <div id="PN" style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always">
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">46</font></div>
        <div style="WIDTH: 100%; TEXT-ALIGN: center">
          <hr style="COLOR: black" noshade size="2">
        </div>
      </div>
      <div id="HDR">
        <div id="GLHDR" style="WIDTH: 100%" align="right">
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">On a
quarterly basis, the Chief Financial Officer reviews the current status of
various loan assets in order to evaluate the adequacy of the allowance for loan
losses.&#160;&#160;In this evaluation process, specific loans are analyzed to
determine their potential risk of loss.&#160;&#160;This process includes all
loans, concentrating on non-accrual and classified loans.&#160;&#160;Each
non-accrual or classified loan is evaluated for potential loss
exposure.&#160;&#160;Any shortfall results in a charge to the allowance if the
likelihood of loss is evaluated as probable. To determine the adequacy of
collateral on a particular loan, an estimate of the fair market value of the
collateral is based on the most current appraised value
available.&#160;&#160;This appraised value is then reduced to reflect estimated
liquidation expenses.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">The
results of this quarterly process are summarized along with recommendations and
presented to executive management for their review.&#160;&#160;Based on these
recommendations, loan loss allowances are approved by executive
management.&#160;&#160;All supporting documentation with regard to the
evaluation process, loan loss experience, allowance levels and the schedules of
classified loans are maintained by the Chief Financial Officer.&#160;&#160;A
summary of loan loss allowances is presented to the Board of Directors on a
quarterly basis.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We have a
concentration of loans secured by real property located in New
Jersey.&#160;&#160;As a substantial amount of our loan portfolio is
collateralized by real estate, appraisals of the underlying value of property
securing loans are critical in determining the amount of the allowance required
for specific loans.&#160;&#160;Assumptions for appraisal valuations are
instrumental in determining the value of properties.&#160;&#160;Overly
optimistic assumptions or negative changes to assumptions could significantly
impact the valuation of a property securing a loan and the related allowance
determined.&#160;&#160;The assumptions supporting such appraisals are carefully
reviewed by management to determine that the resulting values reasonably reflect
amounts realizable on the related loans.&#160;&#160;Based on the composition of
our loan portfolio, we believe the primary risks are increases in interest
rates, a decline in the economy generally, and a decline in real estate market
values in New Jersey.&#160;&#160;Any one or combination of these events may
adversely affect our loan portfolio resulting in increased delinquencies, loan
losses and future levels of loan loss provisions.&#160;&#160;We consider it
important to maintain the ratio of our allowance for loan losses to total loans
at an adequate level.&#160;&#160;Factors such as current economic conditions,
interest rates, and the composition of the loan portfolio will effect our
determination of the level of this ratio for any particular period.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
allowance for loan losses in recent years reflects probable future losses
resulting from the actual growth in our loan portfolio.&#160;&#160;We recognize
that our overall delinquencies, impaired loans and nonaccrual loans have
increased significantly over the past two years.&#160;&#160;We believe the ratio
of the allowance for loan losses to total loans at June 30, 2009 adequately
reflects our portfolio credit risk, given our emphasis on multi-family and
commercial real estate lending and current market conditions.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Although
we believe we have established and maintained the allowance for loan losses at
adequate levels, additions may be necessary if future economic and other
conditions differ substantially from the current operating
environment.&#160;&#160;Although management uses the best information available,
the level of the allowance for loan losses remains an estimate that is subject
to significant judgment and short-term change.&#160;&#160;In addition, the FDIC
and the Department, as an integral part of their examination process, will
periodically review our allowance for loan losses.&#160;&#160;Such agencies may
require us to recognize adjustments to the allowance based on its judgments
about information available to them at the time of their
examination.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Deferred Income
Taxes</font>.&#160;&#160;We use the asset and liability method of accounting for
income taxes.&#160;&#160;Under this method, deferred tax assets and liabilities
are recognized for the future tax consequences attributable to differences
between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and
liabilities and their respective tax bases.&#160;&#160;Deferred tax assets and
liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply to taxable
income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be
recovered or settled.&#160;&#160;If current available information raises doubt
as to the realization of the deferred tax assets, a valuation allowance may be
established.&#160;&#160;We consider the determination of this valuation
allowance to be a critical accounting policy because of the need to exercise
significant judgment in evaluating the amount and timing of recognition of
deferred tax liabilities and assets, including projections of future taxable
income.&#160;&#160;These judgments and estimates are reviewed on a continual
basis as regulatory and business factors change.&#160;&#160;A valuation
allowance for deferred tax assets may be required if the amounts of taxes
recoverable through loss carry backs decline, or if we project lower levels of
future taxable income.&#160;&#160;Such a valuation allowance would be
established through a charge to income tax expense that would adversely affect
our operating results.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Asset Impairment
Judgments</font>.&#160;&#160;Some of our assets are carried on our consolidated
balance sheets at cost, fair value or at the lower of cost or fair
value.&#160;&#160;Valuation allowances or write-downs are established when
necessary to recognize impairment of such assets.&#160;&#160;We periodically
perform analyses to test for impairment of such assets.&#160;&#160;In addition
to the impairment analyses related to our loans discussed above, another
significant impairment analysis is the determination of whether there has been
an other-than-temporary decline in the value of one or more of our
securities.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">Our
available-for-sale securities portfolio is carried at estimated fair value, with
any unrealized gains or losses, net of taxes, reported as accumulated other
comprehensive income or loss in stockholders&#8217; equity.&#160;&#160;Our
held-to-maturity securities portfolio, consisting of debt securities for which
we have a positive intent and ability to hold to maturity, is carried at
amortized cost.&#160;&#160;We conduct a periodic review and evaluation of the
securities portfolio to determine if the value of any security has declined
below its cost or amortized cost, and whether such decline is
other-than-temporary.&#160;&#160;If such decline is deemed other-than-temporary,
we would adjust the cost basis of the security by writing down the security to
fair market value through a charge to current period operations.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Stock-Based
Compensation</font>.&#160;&#160;We recognize the cost of employee services
received in exchange for awards of equity instruments based on the grant-date
fair value of those awards in accordance with SFAS No. 123(R).</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">We
estimate the per share fair value of option grants on the date of grant using
the Black-Scholes option pricing model using assumptions for the expected
dividend yield, expected stock price volatility, risk-free interest rate and
expected option term.&#160;&#160;These assumptions are subjective in nature,
involve uncertainties and, therefore, cannot be determined with
precision.&#160;&#160;The Black-Scholes option pricing model also contains
certain inherent limitations when applied to options that are not traded on
public markets.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">The per
share fair value of options is highly sensitive to changes in assumptions. In
general, the per share fair value of options will move in the same direction as
changes in the expected stock price volatility, risk-free interest rate and
expected option term, and in the opposite direction as changes in the expected
dividend yield. For example, the per share fair value of options will generally
increase as expected stock price volatility increases, risk-free interest rate
increases, expected option term increases and expected dividend yield decreases.
The use of different assumptions or different option pricing models could result
in materially different per share fair values of options.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify">&#160;</div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman">At the
Special Meeting of Stockholders of the Company held on April 22, 2008, the
stockholders of the Company approved the Oritani Financial Corp. 2007 Equity
Incentive Plan authorizing the issuance of 2,781,878 shares of Company common
stock, of which 1,987,055 were authorized as incentive and non-statutory stock
options.&#160;&#160;On May 7, 2008, stock options totaling 1,788,349 were
granted.&#160;&#160;An additional 70,000 options were granted on November 21,
2008.&#160;&#160;The accounting uncertainty described above effects the
remaining 128,706 options that have not yet been granted.</font></div><br>

income increased by $16.8 million, or 23.5%, to $88.4 million, from $71.6
million for the year ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The largest increase was in
interest on mortgage loans.&#160;&#160;Interest on mortgage loans increased by
$17.1 million, or 31.1%, to $72.2 million for the year ended June 30, 2009, from
$55.1 million for the year ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;A critical component
of the Company&#8217;s strategic plan continues to be sound loan
growth.&#160;&#160;The average balance of loans, net increased $323.2 million
while the yield on the portfolio decreased 31 basis points.&#160;&#160;The yield
on the portfolio in 2009 was negatively impacted by interest on nonaccrual
loans.&#160;&#160;On a normalized basis (inclusive of interest in nonaccrual
loans), the yield remained stable.&#160;&#160;Interest on federal funds sold and
short term investments decreased by $1.6 million to $73,000 million for the year
ended June 30, 2009, from $1.7 million for the year ended June 30,
2008.&#160;&#160;The decrease is related to a $20.3 million decrease in the
average balance and a decrease in yield of 347 basis points.&#160;&#160;The
Federal Open Market Committee has significantly decreased the federal funds
target rate over the period.&#160;&#160;While the Company seeks to prudently
deploy cash inflows as quickly as possible, the significant growth in deposits
has increased liquidity above an optimal level.&#160;&#160;The Company&#8217;s primary
asset investment has been loans.&#160;&#160;However, for this period, deposit
growth outpaced loan growth.&#160;&#160;Excess cash flows were initially
invested in MBS AFS.&#160;&#160;Over the course of the year, as the risk/reward
profiles of the investment options changed, and the current and projected cash
needs of the Company changed, the primary investment vehicle for the excess cash
became securities AFS.&#160;&#160;Interest on MBS AFS increased by $2.3 million
to $7.0 million for the year ended June 30, 2009, from $4.7 million for the year
ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The average balance increased $54.7 million
while the yield decreased 34 basis points.&#160;&#160;Interest on the other
investment related captions of securities HTM, securities AFS and MBS HTM
decreased by $972,000, or 9.6%, to $9.2 million for the year ended June 30,
2009, from $10.1 million for the year ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;&#160;The
decrease was primarily due to a decrease in the combined average balance of
$10.8 million and a decreased yield.</font></div>

    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Interest
Expense.</font> Total interest expense increased by $7.3 million, or 19.6%, to
$44.5 million for the year ended June 30, 2009, from $37.2 million for the year
ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The vast majority of the increase was due to
borrowings as interest expense on deposits increased by $397,000 while interest
expense on borrowings increased by $6.9 million.&#160;&#160;The average balance
of deposits increased 27.0% to $880.8 million for the year ended June 30, 2009
from $693.3 million for the year ended June 30, 2008. The cost of deposits
decreased to 2.75% for the year ended June 30, 2009 from 3.44% for the year
ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The average balance of borrowings increased to
$505.6 million for the year ended June 30, 2009 from $310.2 million for the year
ended June 30, 2008. The cost of borrowings decreased to 4.00% for the year
ended June 30, 2009 from 4.30% for the year ended June 30, 2008.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Net interest
income.&#160;&#160;</font>Net interest income increased by $9.5 million, or
27.8%, to $43.9 million for the year ended June 30, 2009, from $34.4 million for
the year ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The Company&#8217;s net interest income and
net interest rate spread were both negatively impacted for the year ended June
30, 2009 due to the reversal of accrued interest income on loans delinquent more
than 90 days.&#160;&#160;The total of such income reversed was $3.7 million for
the year ended June 30, 2009 compared to $521,000 for the year ended June 30,
2008.&#160;&#160;The Company&#8217;s net interest rate spreads for the years ended
June 30, 2009 and June 30, 2008 were 2.36% and 2.06%, respectively.</font></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt"><br></div>
    <div style="DISPLAY: block; MARGIN-LEFT: 0pt; TEXT-INDENT: 0pt; MARGIN-RIGHT: 0pt" align="justify"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman"><font style="DISPLAY: inline; FONT-WEIGHT: bold; FONT-STYLE: italic">Provision for
Loan Losses.&#160;&#160;</font>The Company recorded provisions for loan losses
of $9.9 million for the year ended June 30, 2009 as compared to $4.7 million for
the year ended June 30, 2008.&#160;&#160;The Company charged off a total of $2.7
million in loans during the year ended June 30, 2009 related to losses deemed
probable.&#160;&#160;There were no recoveries in any of the
periods.&#160;&#160;The Company&#8217;s allowance for loan losses is analyzed
quarterly and many factors are considered, including comparison to peer reserve
levels.&#160;&#160;As in prior periods, loan growth was a component of the
provision for loan losses in the 2009 periods.&#160;&#160;The delinquency and
nonaccrual totals, however, were the primary contributors to the increased level
of provision for loan losses</font></div><br>
